sources.text: When relying on Serializable transactions to prevent anomalies, it is important that any data read from a permanent user table not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed. This is true even for read-only transactions, except that data read within a deferrable read-only transaction is known to be valid as soon as it is read, because such a transaction waits until it can acquire a snapshot guaranteed to be free from such problems before starting to read any data. In all other cases applications must not depend on results read during a transaction that later aborted; instead, they should retry the transaction until it succeeds.

Consistent use of Serializable transactions can simplify development. The guarantee that any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions will have the same effect as if they were run one at a time means that if you can demonstrate that a single transaction, as written, will do the right thing when run by itself, you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit. It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies. The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure, but balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments.

13.5. Serialization Failure Handling #

Both Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can produce errors that are designed to prevent serialization anomalies. As previously stated, applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail due to serialization errors. Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure).

In some cases it is also appropriate to retry unique-key failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23505 (unique_violation), and exclusion constraint failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23P01 (exclusion_violation). For example, if the application selects a new value for a primary key column after inspecting the currently stored keys, it could get a unique-key failure because another application instance selected the same new key concurrently. This is effectively a serialization failure, but the server will not detect it as such because it cannot “see” the connection between the inserted value and the previous reads. There are also some corner cases in which the server will issue a unique-key or exclusion constraint error even though in principle it has enough information to determine that a serialization problem is the underlying cause. While it's recommendable to just retry serialization_failure errors unconditionally, more care is needed when retrying these other error codes, since they might represent persistent error conditions rather than transient failures.

It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use. Therefore, PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.

response.evidence_note: The supplied chunks cover SQLSTATE 40001, retrying the whole transaction including all logic deciding which SQL and values, read data validity after abort, and read/write dependency handling in Serializable transactions.

concepts: Retry whole transaction including application logic
expected_steps: Identify that the read value must not be used after the transaction aborts.
Recognize that a serialization_failure has SQLSTATE 40001 and the complete transaction must restart.
Check that retry logic re-runs both the read step and the logic deciding the later write value.
Use the new committed snapshot on retry instead of replaying the old computed value.
Distinguish unconditional retry of 40001 from persistent errors that require more care.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
An online store application uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions. A checkout transaction does the following.

1. Reads the current stock count for an item from a permanent user table.
2. Uses that read value to decide the quantity to write in a later UPDATE.
3. Attempts to commit.

The database aborts the transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure). The application has a retry helper, but the helper only re-executes the UPDATE statement with the quantity value that was computed before the failure; it does not re-run the SELECT or the decision logic that produced that quantity.

Claim:
The retry helper as described is correct because SQLSTATE 40001 means the transaction only needs to replay its write statement, and read-only results can be reused after an abort.

Supporting conditions:
1. The only failure observed is SQLSTATE 40001 from a Serializable transaction.
2. The transaction reads a permanent user table before deciding what value to write.
3. The retry helper replays only the UPDATE with the previously computed quantity.
4. The transaction is not using a deferrable read-only transaction.

Which option best evaluates the claim and the retry design?
options: The claim is correct: 40001 means only the write statement failed, so replaying the UPDATE with the previously computed quantity is safe and avoids repeating the SELECT.

The claim is incorrect: the transaction must retry the complete transaction, including re-running the reads and the logic that decides which values to use, because data read before an abort must not be treated as valid and the retry should use the new committed snapshot.
The claim is correct only if the application first retries SQLSTATE 23505 and SQLSTATE 23P01, because those are the only true serialization failures.
The claim is incorrect because read-only transactions cause serialization conflicts, so the SELECT branch itself must always be retried in a separate read-only transaction.
questions.explanation:
The claim is wrong because a Serializable transaction that reads data and later writes based on that read must restart the whole transaction after a 40001 failure.

Data read before the transaction aborts must not be treated as valid, and the retry should begin with the new committed snapshot.

The retry must include all logic that decides which SQL to issue and which values to use, not just the UPDATE.

The claimed design also ignores the read/write dependency: another transaction may have committed a change that affects both the read and the later write.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must evaluate a concrete retry design under Serializable isolation, connect SQLSTATE 40001 to whole-transaction retry including application decision logic, and reject a design that reuses a read-derived value after an abort.

response.explanation: Serializable transactions can abort with SQLSTATE 40001 because read/write dependencies require rollback to prevent anomalies. Any data read before an abort is not valid for reuse; the application must retry the whole transaction from the beginning, including the SELECT and the decision logic, so the quantity is recomputed from the new committed snapshot. Retrying only the UPDATE with the old value is unsafe and does not satisfy the Serializable retry requirement.

response.evidence_note: Supplied excerpts support all facts used: SQLSTATE 40001, retry whole transaction, reads in deferrable read-only transactions, and care around 23505/23P01.

questions.stem:
An application uses Serializable transactions. A transaction T reads rows from permanent user tables, uses those values to decide which row to update, and then updates that row. Before T commits, the database aborts T with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).

The team proposes the following retry design:
1. Catch only SQLSTATE 40001.
2. On a 40001 error, roll back the current transaction, then create a new transaction and rerun the complete transaction logic from the beginning.
3. Reuse only the new transaction's freshly read values; never depend on values read during the aborted attempt.
4. If a retry again gets SQLSTATE 40001, repeat steps 2 and 3.

Claim: This design is correct for the described transaction and for the general retry rules.

Which option best evaluates the design?

A. Correct, because retrying the complete transaction avoids depending on reads from the aborted transaction and lets the retry see a new initial view.
B. Incorrect, because retrying the complete transaction is unnecessary; reusing the values from the first read is safe since 40001 only rolls back the update.
C. Incorrect, because 40001 must be handled by retrying just the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
D. Correct, but only if the retry is a deferrable read-only transaction, because read-only retries are needed after 40001.

Incorrect, because retrying the complete transaction is unnecessary; reusing the values from the first read is safe since 40001 only rolls back the update.
Incorrect, because 40001 must be handled by retrying just the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
Correct, but only if the retry is a deferrable read-only transaction, because read-only retries are needed after 40001.
questions.explanation:
A is correct. The excerpts state that on 40001 the application should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning, and that this retry sees the previously committed change as part of its initial view. They also state that data read from a permanent user table is not valid until the reading transaction commits, so the retry must not depend on reads from the aborted attempt.

B is wrong: the read values from the aborted attempt are not valid after abort, so they cannot be reused.
C is wrong: retry the complete transaction, not just the failed statement.
D is wrong: the special validity rule concerns reads in a deferrable read-only transaction; the general rule still requires retrying the whole transaction when 40001 occurs.

This is analysis and evaluation rather than recalling a definition.

Recognize that 40001 indicates serialization failure and the required response is to abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning.
Check that the design reruns all logic that decides which SQL to issue or which values to use, as required by the source.
Reject the option that reuses values from the aborted attempt or retries only the failed statement.
Select the option that correctly applies the complete-transaction retry rule to the described transaction.

The team proposes the following retry design:
1. Catch only SQLSTATE 40001.
2. On a 40001 error, roll back the current transaction, then create a new transaction and rerun the complete transaction logic from the beginning.

4. If a retry again gets SQLSTATE 40001, repeat steps 2 and 3.

B. Incorrect, because retrying the complete transaction is unnecessary; reusing the values from the first read is safe since 40001 only rolls back the update.
C. Incorrect, because 40001 must be handled by retrying just the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
D. Correct, but only if the retry is a deferrable read-only transaction, because read-only retries are needed after 40001.

response.title: Evaluating a Serializable Retry Design After a 40001 Error

questions.stem:
An application uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions. While processing a request, it opens a transaction and performs the following steps in order:
1. SELECT the current maximum order_id from the permanent table orders.
2. Compute a new order_id as maximum + 1.
3. INSERT a new row into orders using that computed order_id.

The INSERT then fails with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure). No other statements have run, and nothing has been committed.

The application's current retry logic is:
- On error code 40001, retry only the INSERT statement with the same computed order_id value.

Using only the supplied course material, evaluate this retry design.

Claim: Retrying only the INSERT with the same precomputed value is not a correct retry design for this failure.
Statement 1: For Serializable transactions, data read from a permanent user table must not be considered valid until the transaction that read it has successfully committed; if that transaction aborts, applications must not depend on the read results and instead should retry the transaction until it succeeds.
Statement 2: It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use, and PostgreSQL does not offer automatic retry because it cannot guarantee correctness.
Statement 3: When 40001 occurs, the application should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning; on the second attempt, the transaction will see the previously committed change as part of its initial view of the database.
Statement 4: While it is recommendable to retry serialization_failure errors unconditionally, more care is needed when retrying unique-key or exclusion-constraint failures because they might be persistent rather than transient.

Which option best evaluates the design and follows from the supplied material?
options: The design is correct because 40001 is a transient serialization failure and the same computed order_id will be valid after the INSERT alone is retried.
The design is correct because the SELECT read a permanent user table, and reads from permanent tables remain valid even if the transaction later aborts.
The design is incorrect because the entire transaction must be retried, including recomputing the order_id from prior reads, so the abort discards the validity of the read-derived value.
The design is incorrect only because PostgreSQL already provides automatic retry for 40001, so manual retry is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The read of maximum(order_id) is not valid after the transaction aborts. The material says data read from a permanent table must not be considered valid until commit, and applications must retry the transaction until it succeeds. Retrying only the INSERT with the old computed value ignores the need to redo the logic that chooses which SQL and values to use. The correct response is to abort and retry the whole transaction from the beginning, allowing the second attempt to see the committed changes as part of its initial view. Option C states this evaluation. Options A and B contradict the commit-validity rule. Option D appeals to automatic retry, which the material explicitly says PostgreSQL does not offer.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires integrating the commit-validity rule for reads, the whole-transaction retry rule, and the absence of PostgreSQL automatic retry to evaluate a concrete retry design for read-dependent writes. It is not a definition recall item because the student must judge why retrying only the INSERT with the same value is wrong under the stated 40001 scenario.

expected_steps: Recognize that the maximum(order_id) read is not valid because the transaction aborted.
State that the full transaction must be retried, including logic that decides SQL and values.
Explain that retrying only the INSERT with the same precomputed order_id avoids recomputing the read-dependent value.
Reject the claim that the read remains valid or that PostgreSQL provides automatic retry.

questions.stem:
An application uses Serializable transactions. A transaction T reads rows from permanent user tables, uses those values to decide which row to update, and then updates that row. Before T commits, the database aborts T with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).

The team proposes the following retry design:
1. Catch only SQLSTATE 40001.
2. On a 40001 error, roll back the current transaction, then create a new transaction and rerun the complete transaction logic from the beginning.
3. Reuse only the new transaction's freshly read values; never depend on values read during the aborted attempt.
4. If a retry again gets SQLSTATE 40001, repeat steps 2 and 3.

Claim: This design is correct for the described transaction and for the general retry rules.

Which option best evaluates the design?

A. Correct, because retrying the complete transaction avoids depending on reads from the aborted transaction and lets the retry see a new initial view.
B. Incorrect, because retrying the complete transaction is unnecessary; reusing the values from the first read is safe since 40001 only rolls back the update.
C. Incorrect, because 40001 must be handled by retrying just the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
D. Correct, but only if the retry is a deferrable read-only transaction, because read-only retries are needed after 40001.

Incorrect, because retrying the complete transaction is unnecessary; reusing the values from the first read is safe since 40001 only rolls back the update.
Incorrect, because 40001 must be handled by retrying just the failed statement, not the whole transaction.
Correct, but only if the retry is a deferrable read-only transaction, because read-only retries are needed after 40001.

sources.text: When relying on Serializable transactions to prevent anomalies, it is important that any data read from a permanent user table not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed. This is true even for read-only transactions, except that data read within a deferrable read-only transaction is known to be valid as soon as it is read, because such a transaction waits until it can acquire a snapshot guaranteed to be free from such problems before starting to read any data. In all other cases applications must not depend on results read during a transaction that later aborted; instead, they should retry the transaction until it succeeds.

Consistent use of Serializable transactions can simplify development. The guarantee that any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions will have the same effect as if they were run one at a time means that if you can demonstrate that a single transaction, as written, will do the right thing when run by itself, you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit. It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies. The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure, but balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments.

13.5. Serialization Failure Handling #

Both Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can produce errors that are designed to prevent serialization anomalies. As previously stated, applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail due to serialization errors. Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure).

In some cases it is also appropriate to retry unique-key failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23505 (unique_violation), and exclusion constraint failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23P01 (exclusion_violation). For example, if the application selects a new value for a primary key column after inspecting the currently stored keys, it could get a unique-key failure because another application instance selected the same new key concurrently. This is effectively a serialization failure, but the server will not detect it as such because it cannot “see” the connection between the inserted value and the previous reads. There are also some corner cases in which the server will issue a unique-key or exclusion constraint error even though in principle it has enough information to determine that a serialization problem is the underlying cause. While it's recommendable to just retry serialization_failure errors unconditionally, more care is needed when retrying these other error codes, since they might represent persistent error conditions rather than transient failures.

It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use. Therefore, PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.
